package_info.package_manager: Windows (malicious dropper distributed via phishing archive)
package_info.why_malicious: The package is a multi-stage Windows dropper distributed via phishing, leveraging social engineering, file masquerading, DLL sideloading, and obfuscated configuration files to download and execute additional payloads. This enables remote code execution, persistence, and further malware deployment on the victim's system, while evading detection through the use of renamed legitimate binaries and decoy documents.

execution_context.file_location: !PENTING_LIST OF OFFICERS.rar / 062023_PENTING_LIST OF SUPERVISORY OFFICERS WHO STILL HAVE NOT REPORT.pdf.exe

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Executable masquerading as a PDF: 062023_PENTING_LIST OF SUPERVISORY OFFICERS WHO STILL HAVE NOT REPORT.pdf.exe
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Upon user execution, the disguised executable initiates multiple file drops (including decoy and malware components), writes these files to disk, and launches the infection chain, resulting in the deployment of additional malicious binaries.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: A file with a double extension (.pdf.exe) is crafted to deceive users into believing it is a harmless document, while it is actually an executable. This is a classic social engineering technique to bypass user caution and security controls.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal PDF files do not execute code or drop additional files; this file abuses user trust and Windows' default behavior of hiding known file extensions, making it appear as a legitimate document.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There are no legitimate scenarios where software intentionally uses double extensions to disguise executables as documents.
key_indicators: Large file size inconsistent with typical documents
Drops and executes multiple additional files upon launch
File icon and name mimic legitimate documents

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: IC.exe reaches out to http://185.225.68.37/jay/nl/VCRUNTIME140_1.dll to download a DLL.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, IC.exe initiates an outbound HTTP connection to a hardcoded IP address, downloads a malicious DLL (VCRUNTIME140_1.dll), and saves it to the local filesystem for subsequent sideloading by another process.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: IC.exe's only observed function is to download a DLL from an external, non-Microsoft server, which is a strong indicator of staged malware delivery.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not download DLLs from untrusted, hardcoded IP addresses at runtime, especially without user interaction or update mechanisms.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Software updaters may download updates, but reputable applications do not fetch DLLs from suspicious or hardcoded IPs outside of secure update channels.
key_indicators: Network connection to hardcoded external IP
Download of DLL to local system outside standard update process
No user notification or consent for download

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Drop and open decoy document: Microsoft Office.doc
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the dropper creates a decoy document in the user's temporary directory and opens it, distracting the user while malicious processes execute in the background.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Dropping and opening a decoy document is a common social engineering tactic to divert user attention from ongoing malicious activity.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate installers or applications do not open unrelated documents as part of their process, especially without clear user intent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some installers may display EULAs or documentation, but not as a decoy to mask malicious actions.
key_indicators: Creation and opening of decoy document
Document unrelated to user's intended action
Timing coincides with background malware execution

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: power.exe decodes and processes obfuscated power.xml, launching seAgnt.exe as specified in the XML Actions tag.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, power.exe reads and decodes an obfuscated XML configuration file (power.xml), parses execution instructions, and programmatically launches seAgnt.exe as specified in the XML Actions tag, continuing the staged infection process.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The use of obfuscated configuration files and automated execution of additional binaries are hallmarks of malware staging and evasion.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software may use XML configs, but does not obfuscate them to hide execution instructions for launching unrelated binaries.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Enterprise software may use XML for configuration, but not for obfuscated instructions to launch unrelated executables.
key_indicators: Automated parsing and execution of next-stage binary
No user interaction required for execution

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when seAgnt.exe is launched by power.exe)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: seAgnt.exe (renamed GameBarFTServer.exe) loads VCRUNTIME140_1.dll via DLL sideloading.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the renamed legitimate Microsoft binary (seAgnt.exe) loads the attacker-supplied VCRUNTIME140_1.dll from the same directory via DLL sideloading, resulting in the execution of malicious code within a trusted process context.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: DLL sideloading is a well-known technique for executing malicious code under the guise of a trusted process, often used to evade security controls.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate binaries should only load trusted, signed DLLs from official sources and standard directories, not attacker-supplied DLLs from non-standard locations.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There are no legitimate use cases for intentionally sideloading attacker-supplied DLLs using renamed system binaries.
key_indicators: Loads unsigned or malicious DLL from local directory
DLL sideloading technique to hijack execution flow

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when VCRUNTIME140_1.dll is loaded by seAgnt.exe)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Malicious VCRUNTIME140_1.dll reaches out to http://185.225.68.37/jay/nl/35g3498734gkb.dat to download additional payload.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When loaded by seAgnt.exe, the malicious DLL establishes an outbound HTTP connection to a hardcoded C2 server, downloads an additional payload (35g3498734gkb.dat, which is a copy of the DLL), and writes it to disk, enabling further payload delivery or persistence.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: A DLL making outbound network connections to download further payloads is highly indicative of malware, especially when the payload is a duplicate DLL for persistence or lateral movement.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate runtime DLLs do not perform network operations or self-update from untrusted sources, nor do they download and execute additional code.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: System DLLs should not perform these actions; legitimate updaters use signed, secure channels and do not self-replicate in this manner.
key_indicators: Outbound connection to hardcoded C2 server
Download and write of additional (identical) DLL payload
Network activity from DLL loaded by trusted process

attack_chain.action: User opens phishing archive and executes disguised dropper executable.
Dropper deploys decoy document, IC.exe, power.exe, power.xml, and seAgnt.exe; opens decoy to distract user.
IC.exe downloads malicious VCRUNTIME140_1.dll from remote server.
power.exe decodes obfuscated power.xml and launches seAgnt.exe.
VCRUNTIME140_1.dll connects to C2 and downloads additional payload (35g3498734gkb.dat).

behavioral_signatures: Execution of files with double extensions (e.g., .pdf.exe) masquerading as documents
Dropping and execution of multiple binaries and decoy documents from a single user action
Creation and opening of decoy documents in temporary directories concurrent with malware deployment
Use of obfuscated XML configuration files to control execution flow
DLL sideloading via renamed legitimate binaries (e.g., GameBarFTServer.exe as seAgnt.exe)
Outbound network connections from DLLs or binaries to hardcoded IPs/domains, especially during process startup
file_indicators: 062023_PENTING_LIST OF SUPERVISORY OFFICERS WHO STILL HAVE NOT REPORT.pdf.exe
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for execution of files with double extensions and unexpected process creation chains involving decoy documents and multiple executables. Detect DLL sideloading by monitoring renamed legitimate binaries (e.g., GameBarFTServer.exe as seAgnt.exe) loading unsigned or suspicious DLLs from non-standard directories. Flag outbound network connections from DLLs or binaries to known malicious IPs/domains, especially during process startup. Alert on the presence or execution of the listed file indicators, particularly in unusual directories such as ProgramData or AppData. Correlate the creation and opening of decoy documents with concurrent deployment of additional binaries to identify staged infection attempts.
